questions.question: Define risk diversification. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Risk diversification is a strategy that involves investing in a variety of financial assets, so
  • you can reduce your exposure to any one specific type of risk. The basic principle behind
  • diversification is that by including a mix of asset types in your portfolio, rather than
  • concentrating on just one, you can reduce the negative effects of market volatility or poor
  • performance by one specific asset.

questions.question: Explain how the term structure of interest rate influences the shape of its yield curve. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• The term structure of interest rates, which is the relationship between interest rates and
  • different maturities, directly forms the yield curve.. The shape of the yield curve—upward-
  • sloping, downward-sloping (inverted), or flat—is a direct visual representation of this term
  • Structure and reflects market expectations for future interest rate.
  • OR
  • A normal upward-sloping curve indicates expectations of economic growth and potentially
  • higher future rates, while an inverted curve suggests the opposite, often signalling an
  • upcoming recession.

questions.question: Differentiate between systematic and unsystematic risk. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Systematic risk is market-wide, inherent to the overall market, and cannot be eliminated
  • through diversification eg: market risk, interest rate risk etc. While unsystematic risk is specific to a
  • company or industry and can be reduced or eliminated through diversification. Eg: business
  • risk , financial risk etc OR
  • Systematic Risk
  • Non-diversifiable / Market / Macroeconomic risk,Caused by economy-wide factors,Macro in
  • nature,Cannot be reduced by diversification,Measured by Beta,Includes market risk, interest rate risk,
  • purchasing power risk etc
  • Unsystematic Risk
  • Diversifiable / Specific / Microeconomic risk,Caused by firm/industry-specific factors,Micro in
  • nature,Can be reduced through diversification,No standard measure like Beta,Includes business
  • risk and financial risk etc (Any 3 differences )

questions.question: What do you mean by residual dividend policy? / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• A business with a residual dividend policy holds zero excess cash at any given point in time.
  • All spare cash must be either reinvested in the business or redistributed among the shareholders.
  • Imperfections in the capital market make it rare for a company to follow a pure residual dividend
  • policy. Most businesses instead follow smooth dividend policies that call for regular dividends
  • that show some correlation with the business’ past and present earnings.

questions.question: Write a short note on the One-Fund Theorem. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• The One Fund Theorem states that all investors will hold the same optimal risky portfolio
  • irrespective of their individual risk preferences. In other words, among all risky assets in the
  • market, there exists one unique efficient risky portfolio that every investor should invest in.
  • Individual investors then combine this optimal risky portfolio with the risk-free asset
  • depending on their risk tolerance. More risk-loving investors will invest more in the risky
  • portfolio, while risk-averse investors will allocate more to the risk-free asset. This theorem
  • simplifies portfolio selection by suggesting that security analysis should mainly focus on
  • identifying this single best risky portfolio, rather than building separate portfolios for each
  • investor.(Any other relevant points)

questions.question: What is the role of the risk-free asset in the CML? / [CO1, CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• The risk-free asset plays a crucial role in the Capital Market Line. It allows investors to combine a
  • risk-free return with a market portfolio. By investing partly in the risk-free asset and partly in the market
  • portfolio, investors can achieve any desired risk–return combination on the CML. Low-risk investors lend
  • (invest) in the risk-free asset, while high-risk investors borrow at the risk-free rate to invest more in the
  • market portfolio.Thus, the risk-free asset helps create a straight-line relationship between risk and
  • return, improving portfolio efficiency and giving all investors access to an optimal portfolio on the
  • CML.

questions.question: Briefly explain Modigliani and Miller theory with taxes. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• The Modigliani-Miller theorem (MsM) was developed in the 1650s by Merton Miller and
  • Franco Modigliani. This important and still relevant theory states that the market value of a
  • company is calculated as the present value of its future earnings and underlying assets. They
  • believed that taxes and government regulations do not contribute to capital structure, and that market
  • value is independent of a company’s capital structure. In 1663, Modigliani and Miller revisited
  • their theorem by incorporating corporate taxes. This adjustment fundamentally changes the
  • conclusion: the value of a firm is no longer independent of its capital structure. Instead, debt
  • financing becomes advantageous due to the tax deductibility of interest payments.

questions.question: Discuss the evolution of derivatives. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Derivatives originated as tools for managing price risks in commodities like agricultural
  • products. The earliest forms of derivative trading were forward contracts, which existed
  • centuries ago for crops and precious metals. Organized derivative markets developed in the 16th
  • century, notably with the establishment of the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) in
  • 1848.Later, standardized futures contracts and regulated exchanges expanded derivative
  • trading. In the late 20th century, financial derivatives such as options, swaps, and index
  • futures emerged, driven by financial market globalization, technological
  • advancements, and the need for sophisticated risk management.(VALUE
  • LIBERALLY)

questions.question: Differentiate between cost of equity and cost of debt. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Cost of equity is the minimum rate of return required by shareholders to compensate for
  • the risk of investing in a company’s equity. Methods to calculate cost of equity include the
  • Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and the Dividend Discount Model (DDM). Students face
  • this concept in ratio analysis and case-based exams. Formula for Cost of Equity Cost of Equity
  • = Risk-free Rate + Beta × (Market Return – Risk-free Rate) Cost of capital is the average rate
  • a firm pays for financing from all capital sources— both equity and debt. It is usually calculated
  • using the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) formula and is central to deciding if a
  • project or investment makes financial sense. Weighted Average Cost of Capital (W ACC)
  • Formula WACC = (E/V) × Cost of Equity + (D/V) × Cost of Debt × (1 – Tax Rate)
  • E = Market value of equity ,D = Market value of debt V = E + D (total capital)

questions.question: Formulate the difference between future contract and forward contract in a derivative market. / [CO1, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Futures and forward contracts are both derivative instruments used for hedging and
  • speculation, but they differ in key aspects. A futures contract is a standardized agreement traded
  • on an organized exchange such as the NSE or CME, where the quantity, quality, and delivery
  • date of the underlying asset are predefined. On the other hand, a forward contract is a
  • customised, private agreement between two parties, usually traded in the over-the- counter
  • (OTC) market, allowing terms to be tailored to the needs of the buyer and seller.
  • In futures contracts, the exchange acts as an intermediary and ensures performance through a
  • clearing house, which reduces counterparty risk. Forward contracts involve high
  • credit risk, as there is no intermediary and the settlement depends solely on the parties involved.
  • Futures contracts require daily settlement, known as mark-to-market, where gains or losses are
  • settled each day, while forward contracts are settled only at maturity. Futures are highly liquid
  • due to active secondary trading on exchanges, whereas forwards are less liquid because they
  • are private agreements and difficult to transfer.
  • Futures prices are transparent and regulated, while forward prices remain confidential. Overall,
  • futures are suitable for traders requiring liquidity and risk reduction, while forwards benefit
  • parties wanting customisation and flexibility.

questions.question: Explain the concept of risk management. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Risk management is the systematic process of identifying, analyzing, and controlling
  • risks that may adversely affect the financial performance or objectives of an organization. In
  • the modern business environment, firms are exposed to various uncertainties such as market
  • risks, credit risks, operational risks, and liquidity risks. Therefore, risk management aims to
  • reduce the impact of these uncertainties and ensure the stability and sustainability of the firm.
  • The first step in risk management is risk identification, where all potential internal and external
  • risks are recognized. After identifying them, the next step is risk assessment which involves
  • measuring the probability and impact of risk using tools like Value at Risk (VaR), scenario
  • analysis, and stress testing. Once the risk is evaluated, firms adopt risk control or mitigation
  • strategies such as diversification, hedging, insurance, and asset-liability management to reduce
  • exposure.
  • Risk management is a continuous process, so firms must regularly monitor risks and update
  • strategies to match changing market conditions. Effective risk reporting and strong governance
  • also help in promoting a sound risk culture within the organization.
  • In conclusion, risk management plays a crucial role in protecting a firm from financial
  • instability, minimizing losses, enhancing investor confidence, and ensuring long-term growth
  • and profitability.

questions.question: "Principal-agent problems are inevitable in large organisations". Do you agree? Justify with examples and solutions. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Yes, principal–agent problems are inevitable in large organizations because the owners
  • (principals) and managers (agents) often have different objectives and unequal access to
  • information. The principals expect managers to work for shareholder wealth maximization, but
  • managers may pursue personal goals such as higher salaries, job security, or perks, leading to
  • conflicts of interest. This occurs mainly due to information asymmetry, lack of proper
  • monitoring, and separation of ownership and control. For example, a manager may
  • invest in unnecessary luxury office facilities or take less risky projects only to protect their
  • position, which may reduce shareholder returns. Similarly, in insurance companies,
  • customers may hide their true health conditions to gain benefits, creating adverse selection.
  • To reduce these issues, organizations use a combination of monitoring mechanisms and
  • incentive alignment . Performance-based compensation, stock options, and profit-sharing
  • encourage managers to act in the best interests of shareholders. Corporate governance
  • practices, independent boards, audits, and transparency in reporting also help minimize
  • agency conflicts. In conclusion, while principal–agent problems cannot be completely
  • eliminated in large firms, they can be effectively managed through proper incentives,
  • accountability systems, and strong governance structures.(Any Other relevant points)

questions.question: Explain the concept of beta and its role in measuring systematic risk. / [CO1, CO3] [6x5 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Measures systematic risk of an asset without leverage.
  • • Shows how much the asset’s returns move relative to the overall market.
  • • Used in capital budgeting to assess project risk independent of financing.
  • • Higher asset beta → more volatile and sensitive to market fluctuations.
  • • Lower asset beta → more stable and less correlated with market movements.
  • • Helps determine appropriate discount rate in valuation decisions.
  • Interpretation of Beta (β)
  • β = 1 → Same risk as market (average sensitivity).
  • β > 1 → More risky than market (high sensitivity).
  • β < 1 → Less risky than market (low sensitivity).
  • β = 0 → No relation to market movements..(Any Other relevant points)
